title: The Mystery of Day and Night Animals

pages.text: The Mystery of Day and Night Animals

In the bright morning light, the squirrel leaped from branch to branch. ‘Animals that are active during the day are called diurnal,’ Ranger Nina explained. Rabbits, squirrels, butterflies, and many birds are diurnal. Daytime helps them find food, see clearly, and stay safe. ‘So diurnal means awake in the day,’ Leo said. ‘Exactly,’ said Ranger Nina.

As evening came, the owl opened its wide eyes. ‘Animals that are active at night are called nocturnal,’ said Ranger Nina. Owls, bats, raccoons, and many foxes are nocturnal. The cool dark night is the best time for them to hunt or explore. ‘So nocturnal means awake at night,’ Mia said. ‘Yes,’ Ranger Nina replied.

‘Nocturnal animals often have special features,’ Ranger Nina explained. The owl’s large eyes and sharp hearing help it in the dark. Diurnal animals use daylight to spot food and move quickly. Each animal body is suited for the time it is most active. ‘Mystery clue!’ Leo said. ‘Their bodies match their schedule.’ Ranger Nina laughed. ‘That’s right.’

The sun set, and the park changed. The squirrel tucked into its nest. The owl watched the moonlit pond. ‘Diurnal animals are awake mostly in the day,’ said Mia. ‘Nocturnal animals are awake mostly at night,’ said Leo. ‘And both are perfectly designed for their own time,’ Ranger Nina said. ‘Mystery solved!’

Diurnal animals are most active during the day. Examples include squirrels, rabbits, butterflies, and many birds. Nocturnal animals are most active at night. Examples include owls, bats, raccoons, and many foxes. Nocturnal animals may have large eyes, strong hearing, or a sharp sense of smell. Simple idea: some animals are built for sunshine, and some are built for moonlight.
